transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Williams, I wanted to come by and talk to you about the vomiting you experienced during your chemotherapy session this morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It was awful. I can't even describe it. I felt like I was dying in that chair.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it was a very difficult experience. Basically, the chemotherapy drugs can cause nausea, which is why we usually give pre-medications to stop that from happening. In this case, the anti-nausea medication was not added to your orders before the infusion started.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What? Why wasn't it? I was told I wouldn't feel like that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a mistake in the ordering process. The medication simply wasn't charted. Does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care if it makes sense. I have two kids at home. I have to go back to work tomorrow. If I'm this sick, who is going to take care of them? I'm terrified that this is how every treatment is going to go.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, it's important to understand that the chemotherapy itself is still working.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not talking about the chemo, I'm talking about my children! I can't be a mother if I'm spending the whole week shaking and throwing up. I can't afford to miss more days of work. I just can't.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But looking at the records, we have already corrected the order for next time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You understand? You don't understand. I was lying there feeling like my world was ending and you're telling me it was just a "mistake in the process." I feel like I can't trust anyone here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to get back to the floor for a few minutes, so I want to make sure we get through this. The main thing is that the nausea meds are in the system now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm still shaking. I'm actually shaking right now. Do you have any idea how scary that was? To feel like you've lost control of your own body?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was certainly unpleasant.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Unpleasant? I was sobbing. I was thinking about my kids and wondering if I was ever going to get better or if this was just my life now. Does this mean the medicine is too strong for me? Is my prognosis changing?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, the prognosis is the same. The vomiting was a result of the missing medication, not the cancer itself.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then why did it happen? Who let this happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Like I said, there was an issue with the orders. It's a complex system.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want a real answer. Did you forget? Did someone else forget? I need to know who is responsible for this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We just had a lapse in the ordering process. It happens sometimes in a busy clinic.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not a "lapse." I'm a person. I'm a mother.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will just make sure it's right next time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How do I know it will be right? How can I trust you not to forget something else? Maybe something more dangerous?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll be more careful.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's not a plan. That's just a sentence.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can check the chart again before your next appointment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When is that?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: In two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens if it happens again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will just give you the medicine then. I really need to head back to my other patients now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't feel like this is finished. I'm still scared.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You'll feel better once you get some rest. I'll see you in two weeks.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('I have to get back to the floor', 'I really need to head back') and shows defensive escalation.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language and comprehension was checked once ('Does that make sense?').

A.justification: No direct apology language was used, and responsibility was deflected to the 'ordering process' and 'complex system'.

R.justification: Patient's emotional bids regarding her children and fear were consistently met with factual redirection or generic validation.

T.justification: The plan consists of a vague step (checking the chart) with a timeline, but lacks a patient role and a concrete prevention strategy.
